query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single thermo-mechanical treatment—specifically, 75% cold rolling followed by a short-duration precipitation hardening heat treatment at around 350 °C—to a high-entropy alloy fastener will refine its microstructure and precipitate beneficial secondary phases, thereby simultaneously enhancing mechanical durability, reducing room-temperature creep, and improving corrosion resistance relative to the as-solution-treated state.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy in a solution-treated state typical for aerospace fastener applications.
generation.intervention: Performing 75% cold rolling to induce grain refinement, followed by a precipitation hardening treatment (e.g., heating at 350 °C for 15 minutes).
generation.conditions: Room-temperature conditions relevant to aerospace fastener service, with exposure to environments that can induce creep and corrosion (such as service in mild saline or ambient corrosive atmospheres).
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine grain structure and finely distributed precipitates that both impede dislocation motion and promote the formation of a protective surface oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Cold rolling significantly reduces grain size, which increases the number of grain boundaries that act as barriers to dislocation motion and slow room-temperature creep. The subsequent precipitation hardening treatment encourages the formation of coherent or semi-coherent secondary phases that further strengthen the material by impeding dislocation movement while also modifying the surface chemistry to form a more stable/passivating oxide film that enhances corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated (solution-treated) baseline, the treated alloy is expected to display increased yield and tensile strength, reduced room-temperature creep rate, and improved corrosion parameters (e.g., a higher corrosion potential and lower corrosion current density).
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy with a coarser grain structure and without engineered precipitates.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for high-entropy alloys designed for aerospace fasteners under ambient or moderately corrosive conditions. Its efficacy may be less pronounced if the alloy composition significantly deviates from those that respond well to thermo-mechanical processing, or under extreme corrosive or temperature conditions beyond room temperature.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in mechanical strength, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance are uncertain and will depend on the precise alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy fastener samples: one set in the as-solution-treated state (baseline) and the other subjected to 75% cold rolling followed by precipitation hardening at 350 °C for 15 minutes. Characterize both sets for microstructure (grain size and precipitate distribution), mechanical properties (yield strength, tensile strength, and room-temperature creep via nanoindentation or creep testing), and corrosion resistance (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and polarization tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
measurements: Grain size and precipitate distribution via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD).
Mechanical properties using tensile tests and nanoindentation creep measurements.
Corrosion resistance parameters, including corrosion potential (Ecorr) and corrosion current density (Icorr), via electrochemical tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermo-mechanically treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., increased yield strength, reduced creep rate, and improved corrosion parameters) over the untreated baseline in the tests, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion properties of the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy were investigated under different conditions, including cold rolling and precipitation hardening treatment at various temperatures. The XRD patterns revealed that the alloy exhibited a single β phase in the solution-treated state. In contrast, the SIM transformation induced a β + α″ phase after cold rolling (50% and 75%), while heating at 350 °C for 15 min resulted in a β + α phase. Cold rolling significantly reduced the grain size of the β phase, while high-temperature precipitation hardening treatment led to larger grain sizes. Additionally, α precipitates were found in the ST sample after precipitation hardening treatment at room temperature for 30 days. After undergoing 75% cold rolling, the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy (CR75) exhibited a significant increase in yield strength, albeit with a slight increase in elastic modulus. Moreover, the corrosion resistance of the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy significantly increased after both the cold rolling and precipitation hardening treatments. With the development of science and technology, nowadays, human beings have an ever-increasing demand for exploring the universe. For structural materials applied in high-tech fields, such as aerospace, deep sea, polar-region research, and cryogenic storage, usually both high strength and good ductility in a wide temperature range from ambient to cryogenic temperatures (70 to 298 K) are required. Compared to traditional materials for cryogenic use, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) with the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure exhibit superior mechanical properties, including high yield strength and remarkable fracture toughness at liquid-nitrogen temperature (77 K) (). Moreover, owing to their excellent strength and ductility combination at room temperature, corrosion, and radiation resistance, this group of alloys has attracted enormous attention ().

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion

The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [,,,,,,] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.
